name: ottoni_b1_point_one
canonical_text: Ottoni and colleagues’ 2016 qualitative study looked at three nearby Vancouver neighborhoods. It used seated and walk-along interviews at two time points, with 28 participants in 2012 and 22 in 2014. Its phrase “benches become like porches” captures a wider idea: one place can support both a pause and casual social contact.

name: malmo_triangeln_b1_point_two
canonical_text: Hostile architecture can include sloped benches, center armrests, or outright removal. At Malmö’s Triangeln station, a tilted bench led to a complaint reported on March 4, 2011; officials said it had arrived too steeply and was later corrected. In New York, a 2021 post said subway benches were being removed to stop homeless people sleeping, but it was deleted and the MTA called it an error.

name: boavida_a2_full_story_part2
canonical_text:
A separate review by Boavida and colleagues in 2023 examined 28 articles published from 2020 to 2023. It looked at public parks, active aging, and well-being. The review reported that older park users wanted more benches, and this preference was linked with relaxation.

But benches are not always treated as invitations. Some cities have used defensive, or hostile, design. This can mean sloped seats, center armrests, or removing benches. These changes may make it harder to sleep or lie down.

So one small object now sits inside a larger city question:

“Is public space only for moving through, or is it also for stopping and staying?”

name: comment_2_cancelling
canonical_text: Part 1 showed that cancelling a subscription can involve extra steps, a kind of friction called sludge. Now, listen for how US regulators tried to address this problem, and what later happened to their rule.

name: full_story_part2_click_to_cancel
canonical_text:
On October 16, 2024, it finalized its Click-to-Cancel rule. It covered auto-renewing subscriptions, free trials that become paid plans, and continuing product deliveries.

Its main message was simple:

Canceling should be about as easy as signing up.

If someone joined online, there should be a simple online way to leave. The rule also called for clear key terms, separate consent, no false statements about important facts, and consent records kept for at least three years.

The plan followed a March 2023 proposal and more than 16,000 public comments.

But the legal story changed.

On July 8, 2025, the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals canceled the full 2024 rule because of problems with the rule-making process. This followed a challenge from industry groups.

After that decision, FTC guidance returned to the narrower Negative Option Rule from the 1973 era. The broad Click-to-Cancel rule is therefore no longer in place.

name: katz_shapiro_a2_full_story_part1
canonical_text:
At first, the plan sounds strange: lose money now, grow fast, and think about profit later.

But for some startups, user growth can change the product itself. This happens when a business has a network effect.

Think of a service that helps people connect. When more people join, the service can become more useful for each person. Katz and Shapiro explained this idea as “network externalities” in their 1985 work.

Then a powerful circle can begin.

More users create more value. More value attracts more users.

An early lead can build on itself and become a lasting advantage. A late start can also become a bigger problem over time. In such a market, even the product with the best technology may not win.

This is why speed can be a rational choice. Pete Flint of NFX wrote in 2020 that a company with a true network effect may first run at a loss. It tries to reach a large enough network before rivals do. After that, it may be able to move into profit.
